quartiers:The Rum quarter.name: The Rum quarter
quartiers:The Rum quarter.teaser: North of the dividing street, a quarter rebuilt in straight lines after the fire of 1874
quartiers:The Rum quarter.story: Officially this is Cumhuriyet Mahallesi, but everyone still calls it the Rum quarter. It is where the island's churches and chapels stand, and its lanes run straight because they were laid out again after the fire of 1874. The tallest house put up in the years just after the fire, built in 1876 by Dimosten Tulmidis, now holds the island museum. Under the bell tower of St Mary the stone houses rise two storeys to wooden bays and shutters, and bougainvillea spills off the walls. On a late October evening most guesthouses are shuttered, and you smell woodsmoke and grilled fish from the few kitchens still lit.
quartiers:The Rum quarter.why: Walk it after the day-trippers have gone, when the straight lanes run empty down to the bell tower.
facts: The 19th-century street grid, the stone houses with wooden bays, and the guesthouses, galleries and wine bars
Early evening, when the lanes empty and the stone takes on the last light
The bell tower of St Mary, and the 1876 Tulmidis house that holds the island museum
Asmalı Meyhane, Sandal, Ada'm or Dört Hanımeli; many island kitchens close from October or November to spring, so ask your guesthouse which are open

quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.name: The Turkish mahalle
quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.teaser: South of the dividing street: the lanes the fire missed, two mosques and a plane-tree fountain
quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.story: Alaybey Mahallesi is the half of town the 1874 fire did not reach, so its lanes still bend the way they did before. Here are the mosques and fountains, where the Rum quarter has its churches. Alaybey Camii is the puzzle: its inscription is lost, and nobody can say for sure who built it or when. The Köprülü Mehmet Paşa mosque is easier to date. The grand vizier had it built around 1657, after the castle was taken back from the Venetians, on the site of an older mosque wrecked during their stay. Nearby runs Çınar Çeşme Sokağı, the street named for its plane tree and fountain, with tea glasses on the café tables.
quartiers:The Turkish mahalle.why: Come for the shop counters in the plane-tree lanes by the mosque, open longer into the off-season than the harbour front.
facts: The older, looser street plan, the two mosques and the fountains
Mid-morning, when the shops by the mosque are open and the lanes are in shade

quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.name: The harbour and the castle square
quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.teaser: Where the ferry ties up under the castle walls, and the town opens out from the quay
quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.story: The car ferry from Geyikli's Yükyeri quay crosses the strait and docks beneath the castle, and the town opens out from the quay: fishing boats tied up along the harbour wall, tea glasses on the café tables, the wind coming off the water. Behind the quay is Kale Meydanı, the castle square, where older guides put the weekly producers' market; it has since moved, so ask in town where the stalls stand now. After dark the castle is floodlit and the masts in the harbour stand out against it. In winter, when most of the registered population has left the island, you share the quay with a few fishermen.
quartiers:The harbour and the castle squ.why: Step off the boat at dusk once: the floodlit walls over the masts are the island's picture of itself.
facts: The ferry quay, the fishing boats and the castle square
After dark, for the floodlit walls over the harbour
The view of the walls and the masts together from the end of the quay

curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.name: Tenedos and the wooden horse
curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.teaser: Virgil hid the Greek fleet behind this island while Troy pulled the horse inside its walls
curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.story: 'Est in conspectu Tenedos', Virgil writes in Book 2 of the Aeneid: there is an island in sight of Troy, famous and rich while Priam's kingdom stood, now only a bay and an unsafe anchorage for ships. Aeneas tells it at Dido's table. The Greeks sail to Tenedos and hide on its empty shore, the Trojans think they have gone, and the horse is pulled into the city. The island's own coins tell another story. From about 420 BC Tenedos struck a double-headed axe on its silver, and beside it, again and again, a bunch of grapes.
curiosities:Tenedos and the wooden horse.why: From the town's west side, look across at the Troad coast: the poem's view, read in reverse.
facts: Look across the strait from the harbour to the Troad shore where Troy stood; the island museum keeps coins among its collections

This is literature, not archaeology: no find places the fleet here. The axe has been read as the emblem of a local god, and Cook (1925) tied the grape-and-axe pair to a Dionysiac cult; the stories of Tenes, the island's founder hero, are later, and Cook argued his name was taken from Tenedos, not the other way round

curiosities:The louse that came late.name: The louse that came late
curiosities:The louse that came late.teaser: 'A pre-phylloxera island', say the guides; the sources found do not back them up
curiosities:The louse that came late.story: The line runs through many Bozcaada guides, ours included: the root louse that wiped out Europe's vineyards in the 19th century only reached the island in the 1940s, so its vines are a pre-phylloxera survival. Searched in English and Turkish in October 2026, the claim has no source. What the record does show is the louse reaching the Ottoman Empire early: in Thrace from 1881, then on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, at Kızıltoprak, and around Bursa and Aydın from 1885. The state did not formally admit it until 1886. When it reached Tenedos, and whether the vines stand on their own roots today, no source we found records.
curiosities:The louse that came late.why: Ask a grower in the vines whether his stocks are grafted: the honest answer is worth more than the slogan.
facts: At a cellar door ask whether the vines are grafted or on their own roots, and when the old rows were last replanted

The 1940s arrival date and the 'pre-phylloxera island' label appear in guidebooks only. Ottoman sources put the louse in Thrace from 1881 and in Anatolia from 1885; no source found dates its arrival on Bozcaada or says whether today's vines are grafted

curiosities:Left out of the exchange.name: Left out of the exchange
curiosities:Left out of the exchange.teaser: In 1923 the Greek–Turkish population exchange left out two islands, and Tenedos was one of them
curiosities:Left out of the exchange.story: The Treaty of Lausanne returned Imbros and Tenedos to Turkey, three years after the Treaty of Sèvres had given them to Greece, and wrote a promise into Article 14. The islands would have a special local administration with guarantees for their non-Muslim people, and the Greek–Turkish exchange of populations would not apply to them. So while more than a million people elsewhere were moved, Tenedos's Orthodox families stayed, with their vines and their churches. The promise did not hold. The community dwindled over the century that followed, and how far it fell depends on whose figures you take.
curiosities:Left out of the exchange.why: Behind the Rum quarter's bougainvillea is a treaty clause: read it before you walk those lanes.
facts: The church of St Mary and the Rum quarter's lanes, and the Ayazma chapel on 26 July, when the diaspora comes back for the feast

Numbers differ: our old guide had about 5,420 Greeks in 1912 and about 22 by 2000; one 1923 count gives about 1,631 Greeks on Tenedos; another of our pages said 'close to 2,000, now about twenty'. No single official series was found

culture:The castle.name: The castle
culture:The castle.teaser: Mehmet II's 1455 fortress over the harbour, where a 2023 dig reached Late Bronze Age layers
culture:The castle.story: The walls you see are Ottoman. Mehmet II took the island and rebuilt its fortress in 1455, two years after taking Constantinople. Köprülü Mehmet Paşa and later Mahmud II repaired it. Earlier Venetian and Genoese works were pulled down after the 14th-century War of Chioggia. Inside are an outer bailey, an inner citadel and a dry moat on the landward side; from the ramparts you look down on the harbour and across to the Troad. In 2023 the castle was excavated for the first time, and the team under Prof. Turan Takaoğlu found Byzantine, Roman and Late Bronze Age settlement traces below the Ottoman floor.
culture:The castle.why: Walk the ramparts for the one view that holds the harbour, the two quarters and the strait together.
facts: On the harbour, at the head of the castle square

culture:The church of St Mary.name: The church of St Mary
culture:The church of St Mary.teaser: The Rum quarter's church of 1869 rang its bells again after a two-year restoration
culture:The church of St Mary.story: The Kimisis Theotokou, the church of the Dormition of the Virgin, has served the island's Orthodox since 1869. Inside, five Corinthian columns divide a three-aisled nave; outside, the four-storey bell tower stands over the Rum quarter's roofs, and you can see it from most of town. After a two-year restoration the church reopened for worship, and the bells rang for a liturgy led by the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew. The mayor and the island's mufti came, and so did Orthodox families from several countries. Its feast is the Dormition, 15 August.
culture:The church of St Mary.why: Go in quietly on an ordinary morning, when it is still a parish church before it is a sight.
facts: The Rum quarter (Cumhuriyet Mahallesi), under its bell tower
An active church; visiting hours not published, so try the door and respect services

culture:The island museum.name: The island museum
culture:The island museum.teaser: One collector's maps, coins and wine bottles in the tallest house built after the 1874 fire
culture:The island museum.story: The Bozcaada Yerel Tarih Araştırma Merkezi, the Local History Research Centre, fills a house that Dimosten Tulmidis built in 1876. It was the tallest and grandest of the houses put up just after the fire of 1874. The collection is Hakan Gürüney's, an islander who has spent years gathering Bozcaada. There are fossils and archaeological finds, coins, old maps and engravings of Tenedos, island wine bottles, and the household goods of Greek and Turkish families side by side. The building was given over to the collection by a 7 June 2006 protocol with the district governorship. On a windy day it is the quickest way to read the island's layers.
culture:The island museum.why: Look for the old island wine labels: the vineyard history in glass and paper, before you walk the rows.
facts: Town centre, in the 1876 Tulmidis house

culture:The windmills.name: The windmills
culture:The windmills.teaser: Rebuilt from islanders' old photographs, the stone mills that once ground the island's wheat
culture:The windmills.story: The island once ground its own wheat in round stone mills along its ridges, and by the late 2010s they were ruins. The district governor İbrahim Gültekin said they had collapsed 50 to 60 years before, from neglect. The district governorship rebuilt them in 2019 from the islanders' memory. Islanders brought out old family photographs to show where each mill had stood, then the sites were cleared and levelled. Two mills, 4 m across and 6.5 m tall, went back up on the island's south side, and a third was under way at the north end. They do not grind. They give the skyline back its old silhouette against the turbines.
culture:The windmills.why: Go up for the silhouette at the end of the day, with the sea and the strait behind the mills.
facts: On the high ground: two on the island's south side, one at the north end

culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.name: Ayazma chapel and spring
culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.teaser: A 1734 chapel under plane trees that opens one day a year, when bread, wine and oil are blessed
culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.story: Ayazma comes from the Greek hagiasma, holy water. The chapel of Aya Paraskevi was built in 1734, attributed to one Manolaki Manolidis, and stands among old plane trees beside a two-spouted fountain that runs all year. For most of the year the door is shut. On 26 July, Saint Paraskevi's day, it opens for the Ayazma Panayırı: islanders and families back from Greece fill the shade, the Metropolitan of Gökçeada and Bozcaada blesses bread, wine and olive oil, and pilgrims light candles and make wishes at the spring. In July 2025 the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew led the service. In October you have the plane trees to yourself.
culture:Ayazma chapel and spring.why: Sit by the running fountain under the planes, the coolest shade on the south coast.
facts: Inland from Ayazma beach on the south coast

walks:Göztepe.name: Göztepe
walks:Göztepe.teaser: The island's high point on foot: vines, pines, the windmills and the islets in one turn of the head
walks:Göztepe.story: Göztepe, the lookout hill, is the top of the island, and the climb is on a path, gentle, through scrub that smells of thyme when the sun is on it. Count about half an hour from the centre. From the top the whole of Bozcaada lies below: the green and rust of the vineyards, the dark pines, the white sails of the rebuilt windmills, the turbine ridge to the west, the islets offshore and the mainland across the strait. The meltem that keeps the vines dry blows hardest up here. By late October the vines below are picked and turning, and a sweater earns its place.
walks:Göztepe.why: Go at the start or the end of the day, when the light lies low across the vineyards.
facts: A gentle footpath to the summit, 192 m by the old guide (not confirmed); the old guide also says no road reaches the top

walks:Polente at sunset.name: Polente at sunset
walks:Polente at sunset.teaser: An hour out along the bare western cape to the 1861 lighthouse, as the turbines turn behind you
walks:Polente at sunset.story: The walk out to Polente is longer than it looks from town: an hour each way, west past the wind farm, over open ground with no tree to stand under. The light at the end has stood on the cape since 1861, a tall white tower of about 30 m. The ridge behind it carries the wind farm that now makes the island's power. The reward comes at the end of the day, when people drive or walk out, sit on the rocks with a beer, and watch the sun drop into the sea beyond the lighthouse.
walks:Polente at sunset.why: Stay until the light comes on: the old tower lit against the turbine ridge is the island's evening.
facts: The full width of the island to the western tip
About 1 hour each way on foot
Road and open track, no shade

Water, a torch for the walk back, a layer against the wind

walks:The vineyard country.name: The vineyard country
walks:The vineyard country.teaser: Low gobelet vines raked by the meltem, from Göztepe's flanks down to the south coast
walks:The vineyard country.story: Between a third and a half of Bozcaada is under vine, and the inland walk is through it. The vines are gobelet bushes, trained low and knuckled close to the dusty ground. They are dry-farmed, and the steady meltem dries the morning damp off the leaves before mildew can take hold. The tracks run open between the rows from below Göztepe to the south coast, Late August into September is the harvest, with the Bağ Bozumu festival at its end. By late October the rows are picked, the leaves go rust and yellow, and the smell of the island's must still hangs around the cellars.
walks:The vineyard country.why: Walk between the rows themselves: the low, wind-shaped vines explain the island's wine better than any glass.
facts: Bozcaada town, taking the tracks inland towards Göztepe
Open-ended: loops of a few kilometres between the rows

calas:Ayazma.name: Ayazma
calas:Ayazma.teaser: The south coast's long sand bay under the chapel, the place to swim when the poyraz blows from the north
calas:Ayazma.story: Ayazma is the beach the whole island means in August: a broad curve of fine pale sand on the south coast, shallow turquoise water, umbrellas in rows and a strip of fish-and-meze places behind it. The bay takes its name from the Aya Paraskevi chapel and spring on the slope above it. On a north wind the sea here lies flat while the north coast churns. Come back in late October and the picture changes: loungers stacked away, the kitchens mostly shuttered, a handful of locals walking dogs along the waterline and the sand to yourself.
calas:Ayazma.why: The calmest big swim on the island on a poyraz day; in high summer claim your patch of sand early in the morning.
facts: Island minibus from town in season (regular in June-September); by car or bike out of season, when a winter minibus is not confirmed

calas:Sulubahçe.name: Sulubahçe
calas:Sulubahçe.teaser: Ayazma's quieter neighbour on the south coast: the same clear water, no loungers, no café
calas:Sulubahçe.story: Walk on from Ayazma's umbrellas and the south coast goes quiet at Sulubahçe. The sand is good and the water as clear, but nobody rents you a lounger or sells you a beer, so the people here are campers, families with a cool box and the occasional snorkeller working the rock shelves at the eastern end. Like the rest of this shore it is a north-wind beach: when the poyraz blows it lies calm, and when the lodos swings in from the south the swell comes straight onto it.
calas:Sulubahçe.why: The south-coast swim without the lounger rows: come for the rock shelves with a mask.

calas:Habbele.name: Habbele
calas:Habbele.teaser: A rounded, shallow bay that stays calm on a poyraz, about 7 km from town
calas:Habbele.story: Habbele is a small, enclosed bay with golden sand, shallow water that warms faster than the open beaches, and a shape that keeps the poyraz swell outside. That makes it the bay families choose in summer: a paid lounger section at one end, a free stretch where you put down your own towel at the other. Look before you step in: sea urchins sit on the rocky patches of the bottom, so water shoes save the afternoon. Out of season the loungers go and it is simply a quiet cove.
calas:Habbele.why: The gentlest water on the island for children and weak swimmers; wear water shoes for the urchins.
facts: About 7 km from town by road; the Ayazma minibus serves it in season

calas:Akvaryum.name: Akvaryum
calas:Akvaryum.teaser: Named for water clear enough to count the fish: the cove to cross to when the lodos turns
calas:Akvaryum.story: Akvaryum means aquarium, and the name is a description: over pale rock and sand the water is clear enough that you watch fish moving below you without a mask. There is nothing else here: no sunbeds, no showers, no changing cabins. The track down is rough, so most people leave the car at the roadside and walk the last stretch, about fifteen minutes. This is the swim for a south (lodos) wind, when the south-coast beaches take the swell and this side lies flatter.
calas:Akvaryum.why: The island's best snorkelling: come on a lodos day with a mask and fins.

calas:Çayır.name: Çayır
calas:Çayır.teaser: The island's wind beach, where Europe's Formula Kite champions raced in June 2015
calas:Çayır.story: Çayır is the beach for people who want the wind. On a flat point on the island's north side it takes the poyraz head-on, and offshore reefs flatten the water inside them, which is why kite racers rate it. From 23 to 28 June 2015 it hosted the IKA Formula Kite European Championships during the Go Bozcaada festival, with riders from about a dozen countries; Britain's Oliver Bridge and Russia's Elena Kalinina kept their titles. On a windy day the sky over the beach fills with kites and the swimmers move to the south coast.
calas:Çayır.why: Watch, or take a lesson: this is not a calm swim, it is where the boards go.

calas:Tuzburnu.name: Tuzburnu
calas:Tuzburnu.teaser: A small rocky cove on the eastern side, with no facilities and clear, cool water
calas:Tuzburnu.story: Tuzburnu, the salt cape, is a swim for people who prefer rock to sand. There is no café, no lounger and no shade, only clear water over stone, colder than the shallow south-coast bays, and a car parked at the end of the road. Older descriptions put it at the western tip under the lighthouse and windmills; that is Polente, a different cape. Tuzburnu lies on the island's eastern side, among the coves that give shelter when the lodos blows from the south.
calas:Tuzburnu.why: A lodos-day alternative to Akvaryum, for a quiet swim off the rocks.

provisioning:The Wednesday market.name: The Wednesday market
provisioning:The Wednesday market.teaser: The week's produce stalls, for island tomatoes, local cheese and jam by the jar
provisioning:The Wednesday market.story: Shop it like a cook: walk the whole market once before you buy, then take tomatoes that smell of the plant, a slab of goat or Ezine cheese, a jar or two of domates reçeli, and in late summer Çavuş grapes by the case. It is a market for islanders, not the souvenir shelves. Bring cash and your own bags.
provisioning:The Wednesday market.why: The one day of the week to buy the island's own produce at source rather than from a shop shelf.

provisioning:Domates reçeli.name: Domates reçeli
provisioning:Domates reçeli.teaser: Tomato jam, the island's sweet preserve, cooked in late summer and sold by the jar all year
provisioning:Domates reçeli.story: Domates reçeli is tomato jam: tomatoes cooked down slowly with sugar until they turn glossy and dark red, sweet, with a faint savoury edge that tells you it was once a vegetable. Turkish food writers trace the recipe to the island's Rum families, and today it is the jar every visitor carries home, next to fig jam, from homes, shops and market stalls. It comes out at breakfast and with cheese. Despite the name on so many labels, it has no geographical indication: the island's registered product is the Çavuş grape, not the jam.
provisioning:Domates reçeli.why: Buy a homemade jar rather than a factory one and taste it with the island's white cheese.
facts: Jam of island tomatoes cooked with sugar; a Rum household recipe; no geographical indication found (Oct 2026)

provisioning:Çavuş grapes.name: Çavuş grapes
provisioning:Çavuş grapes.teaser: A big, pale-gold table grape, protected since 2 June 2020 as Bozcaada Çavuş Üzümü
provisioning:Çavuş grapes.story: Bozcaada Çavuşu is first a grape for eating: big berries, thin pale-gold skin and a sweet, juicy bite. In September 2018 the island's agricultural development cooperative applied to TÜRKPATENT, and on 2 June 2020 the name was registered as a designation of origin, No. 497, for grapes grown in the Bozcaada district. A university study afterwards found the gain was smaller than hoped, because the island lives on summer visitors and the variety is delicate. By late October the harvest is over and the vines are bare.

around:Troy.name: Troy
around:Troy.teaser: The UNESCO-listed mound at Tevfikiye, and the museum built beside it in 2018
around:Troy.story: Troy is a low mound of trenches, walls and ramps on the plain near the mouth of the Dardanelles, cut open layer by layer by excavators since the nineteenth century. UNESCO listed it as World Heritage in 1998. The Troy Museum, chosen in a Ministry of Culture architecture competition won by Ömer Selçuk Baz, opened nearby at Tevfikiye on 10 October 2018. Its seven sections show about 2,000 finds from Troy and the Troad around it, the island included, and in 2020 it received a special commendation in the European Museum of the Year awards.
around:Troy.why: Do the museum first, then the mound: the finds make the trenches readable.

around:Gökçeada.name: Gökçeada
around:Gökçeada.teaser: Imbros: stone Greek villages, olive oil and dibek coffee, by ferry from Kabatepe
around:Gökçeada.story: Gökçeada, Imbros to its Greek families, is Bozcaada's larger partner in history, out beyond the Gallipoli peninsula. Inland from the port at Kuzulimanı the old villages climb the hills: Zeytinliköy (Agios Theodoros), with its stone houses and narrow lanes, and Tepeköy, Kaleköy, Dereköy and Eski Bademli. In Zeytinli the coffee is dibek kahvesi, beans crushed in a stone mortar with a heavy iron pestle, then sieved. Visitors leave with olive oil. There is no ferry from Bozcaada: you go back to the mainland and cross the peninsula to Kabatepe.
around:Gökçeada.why: Take a dibek coffee in Zeytinliköy and buy a can of the island's olive oil.

around:Assos.name: Assos
around:Assos.teaser: A temple of Athena on the acropolis above Behramkale, and a small stone harbour below it
around:Assos.story: Assos is the ancient city above the village of Behramkale, down the coast from Geyikli on the Gulf of Edremit. You climb through the village lanes to the acropolis, where the Temple of Athena stands on the summit with the sea opening below on every side. From there the ruins fall away down the slope towards a small harbour at the water's edge, a separate stop at the bottom of a steep road. The site is run by the Ministry of Culture through the Çanakkale Museum, with free entry for children under eight. Come in the cool of the afternoon: the climb is steep and the hill has little shade.
around:Assos.why: Climb to the temple late in the afternoon, then drive down to the harbour for the evening.

The guide's earlier edition dated the café to 1969; we could not confirm that year. Islanders come for a coffee and a conversation; this is a place for the shade and the people, not a desk, and in the cooler months the canopy thins and the crowd goes with it.

avoid:Coming in winter for the food.name: Coming in winter for the food
avoid:Coming in winter for the food.teaser: From November most kitchens are shuttered; the island you read about runs from spring to October
avoid:Coming in winter for the food.story: Walk the Rum quarter on a late-autumn evening and the lanes that held fifty tables in August are dark: chairs stacked behind glass, vine canopies bare, the meltem rattling a shutter. The island empties after the season and very few businesses stay open through the winter; a TGRT report on the New Year rush found the handful that do, and others reopening only because guests asked. The squid is still in the strait and the wine is still in the cellars, but the long meze evening needs a full room and a full kitchen, and from November you cannot count on either.
avoid:Coming in winter for the food.why: Plan the eating trip for late May, June or September, and treat a winter visit as a walk with a bottle, not a table crawl.
facts: Late October: shutters coming down in the Rum quarter, beach businesses packed away, the ferry already on its reduced winter timetable

avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.name: The car ferry on a summer Friday
avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.teaser: One GESTAŞ line carries every car to the island, and on a holiday weekend everyone tries it at once
avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.story: Everything that reaches Bozcaada by road goes through the pier at Geyikli (Yükyeri) and the GESTAŞ car ferry, a crossing of about 35 minutes. Tickets are sold on the mainland side; there is no ticket office on the island. On long holiday weekends the island fills: in May 2026 the regional press reported it 'doldu taştı', full to overflowing, and bayram bookings close to 100 per cent. The ferry runs hourly in high summer, but from 5 October 2026 the winter timetable cut it to four or five sailings a day, three to four hours apart, so a missed boat now costs an afternoon.
avoid:The car ferry on a summer Friday.why: Leave the car on the mainland and cross on foot on a weekday; the town, the cellars and the near beaches are all within reach without one.

avoid:The harbour-front set menu.name: The harbour-front set menu
avoid:The harbour-front set menu.teaser: The tables built for the tour coaches feed volume; the island's real kitchen is a few lanes back
avoid:The harbour-front set menu.story: Bozcaada's money no longer comes from the bottle but from the day-tripper: the old guide counted well over a million visitors a year and summer rooms near full. Some of the harbour-front tables are set up for exactly that crowd, a fixed run of plates timed to the next ferry, laid out for the group rather than cooked for the person. The fish and the squid on the island come from the same strait whichever door you choose; what changes is whether a cook is watching the grill. Your money goes further at the cellar door, at the Wednesday market and at the meyhanes that cook to order.
avoid:The harbour-front set menu.why: Walk two or three lanes up from the water before you sit down; the meze tables that cook to order are there.

follow:Bozcaada municipality.story: Bozcaada Belediyesi is the island's municipality and the body that has run the September grape-harvest festival since the 1990s. Its website is where official notices go first: job calls, public announcements and the programmes of the events it organises. It is written for islanders, in Turkish, and is plain rather than polished, but when you need to know whether the harvest days or a public event are on, the town hall is the source the travel sites copy from.

follow:The ferry operator.story: GESTAŞ runs the Geyikli to Bozcaada line along with the other Çanakkale island and strait crossings. It is promotional and light on vintages, but it is official, it is in English, and it names the grapes the way the cellar doors will.

listening:No hi-fi listening bar.name: No hi-fi listening bar
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.teaser: No record bar on the island or in Çanakkale that we could find; here the music is live, and seasonal
listening:No hi-fi listening bar.story: We looked for a vinyl or hi-fi listening room on Bozcaada and across the strait in Çanakkale, and found none. An island of about three thousand winter residents does not keep one going. What it has instead is sound you have to be there for: a jazz festival that takes over a monastery yard and a beach for three days in early September, music in the lanes during the harvest days, and in high summer the late bars of the Rum quarter. Out of season the soundtrack is the meltem in the vines and the ferry horn.

listening:Live music on the island.teaser: Three stages in early September: a monastery yard, a beach and a free one in town
listening:Live music on the island.story: The Bozcaada Caz Festivali reached its tenth edition in 2026, on the first weekend of September, under the theme 'Geçicilik', impermanence. It spreads over three stages: the yard of the Ayazma monastery above the south coast, the sand at Habbele, and a free stage at the Salhane in town. The bill runs from jazz to electronic, psychedelic and reggae, with players from the UK, the Netherlands, Germany and France beside Turkish names such as Korhan Futacı and Gevende, plus talks, workshops and walks across the island. Outside that weekend, music is a summer thing; at New Year the few meyhanes and bars that open put on their own nights.

craft:Do this one.teaser: Nothing on the island clears the bar fully; the closest is picking grapes in the rows at harvest
craft:Do this one.story: We searched for a hands-on class proper to Bozcaada with a named maker you can sign up with: ceramics, weaving, jam, cooking, boatbuilding. None turned up. The nearest thing is the harvest itself. During the grape-harvest festival, held from 14 to 23 August in 2026, visitors go out to the vineyards to cut bunches by hand, the Çavuş and Karalahna pruned low against the wind, and the grapes come back to town with music. It is real work in a real crop, open to anyone who turns up, but it is an event, not an apprenticeship: no named master teaches you, and it happens once a year.

craft:What is sold as island-made.name: What is sold as island-made
craft:What is sold as island-made.teaser: 'Island wine' in a plain bottle is not always what it claims: police seized 1,300 litres of fake on Bozcaada
craft:What is sold as island-made.story: The island's reputation sells, and not everything that trades on it is what the label says. In one operation the gendarmerie raided a vineyard house on Bozcaada and seized 1,300 litres of counterfeit wine, with one person detained. Home-batch wine is part of island life, made in small lots for the family, but a plain unlabelled bottle sold over a counter carries no guarantee of grape, maker or safety. The old guide's advice holds for food too: the year-round tourist stalls are not the same thing as the Wednesday producers' market, and the Çavuş grapes and jams are best bought from the people who grow and cook them.

drink:Çavuş.name: Çavuş
drink:Çavuş.teaser: The island's sweetest eating grape, pressed into a dry white
drink:Çavuş.story: Çavuş is the grape Bozcaada eats: islanders call it the most flavourful of the island's table grapes, big, thin-skinned and fragile. The wineries also press it, alone or with Vasilaki, for dry whites and pale rosés. A grape bred for the fruit bowl is not an obvious candidate for a serious wine, which is exactly why the bottles are worth a glass: expect something light and soft rather than sharp, made to drink young with the meze. Corvus and Talay both make one.
drink:Çavuş.why: Ask for a Çavuş white with the first cold meze, before the reds come out.
facts: A light, soft dry white, sometimes a pale rosé; drink it young and cold

drink:Vasilaki.name: Vasilaki
drink:Vasilaki.teaser: A thin-skinned white that ripens early on the island and is drunk young
drink:Vasilaki.story: Vasilaki keeps a Greek name from the island's Rum winemakers. It is a white with thin-skinned berries that ripens early on Bozcaada and goes into both dry and sweet wines; the ministry's grape guide is plain that it is not one for the cellar. Writers describe the dry version as acidic and fuller than you expect, one comparing it to a Chardonnay, nearly. The old guide said it grows nowhere else; the sources we found call it Bozcaada's own but do not go that far. Drink it the year after the harvest, with grilled fish.
drink:Vasilaki.why: If a cellar has a sweet Vasilaki, taste it beside the dry one: the same grape, two directions.
facts: Fresh, acidic, fuller than its colour suggests; dry or sweet

drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.name: Karalahna and Kuntra
drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.teaser: Two island reds: one dark and firm, one light and cherry-red, often in the same bottle
drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.story: Karalahna is late-ripening and grown almost only on Bozcaada: deep-coloured, high in acid, firm in tannin. Even its name is argued over, black pumpkin or black cabbage. Kuntra is the same grape the mainland calls Karasakız (also Mavro Kuntra, Sakız Kara); light, with red cherry and redcurrant, it went mostly into the still for brandy until island producers revived it for reds, rosés and sparkling wines. Each covers the other's gap, which is why the cellars so often blend them, or set Karalahna beside Merlot. Corvus's Corpus is the famous one; ask the cellar door for the plain versions too.
drink:Karalahna and Kuntra.why: Taste a straight Kuntra and a Karalahna blend side by side to understand the island's red.
facts: Karalahna: dark, tannic, high acid. Kuntra: pale, light, red cherry and redcurrant

drink:Rakı.name: Rakı
drink:Rakı.teaser: Not made on the island, but the drink the meze evening is built around
drink:Rakı.story: Bozcaada makes wine; rakı comes from the mainland. Yet under the vine canopies of the meyhanes it is the fixed partner to the cold meze, the raw fish and the grilled squid as they come out in waves. It is an anise spirit, clear in the bottle, that turns cloudy white the moment water goes in. The ritual is slow: a narrow glass, a finger or two of rakı, cold water to cloud it, then ice, and a long evening of small plates between sips. The old guide put it best: the wine is what you take home, the rakı is the meal.
drink:Rakı.why: Order it the island way, with the meze tray, and let the evening run at its pace.
facts: Clear anise spirit that turns milky white with water

bars:Bakkal.teaser: A cocktail bar on a cobbled side lane: quiet by day, a small dancefloor by two in the morning
bars:Bakkal.story: Bakkal means grocer, and the name is the joke: this is one of the few places on the island that turn into a bar after dark. By day it is fresh juice and quiet tables on a cobbled side lane of the Rum quarter; on a summer night it fills with a young crowd, music up, the lane full. The cocktails lean on what grows here: Hürriyet Daily News sent readers for the ones made with corn poppy and with grapes. It is seasonal, so in late October expect it shut until spring.

bars:The wine route.name: The wine route
bars:The wine route.teaser: Two cellar shops in town, the bigger cellar doors out in the vines, all inside one island day
bars:The wine route.story: Close to half of Bozcaada is under vine, dry-farmed and trained low as bushes against the meltem, and the island is small enough that the wine route is the island itself. Start in town, where Talay and Çamlıbağ, two old family houses, pour at their shops among the lanes. Then go out into the vines: Corvus by the rows north-west of town, with limited visiting days, and Amadeus to the south, where the winemaker pours himself. In September the air at the cellars smells of must; in late October the rows are bare, and outside summer the tastings are not guaranteed.
bars:The wine route.why: Do the town shops on foot and hire a car or taxi for the cellar doors out in the vines.
facts: The town centre, at the Talay and Çamlıbağ shops
A day, with lunch in town between the shops and the cellar doors
A native-grape tasting: Çavuş, Vasilaki, Karalahna and Kuntra side by side
Water, a hat, and a car or taxi for Corvus and Amadeus; call ahead in October to April, as winter opening is not confirmed

bars:Çamlıbağ.name: Çamlıbağ
bars:Çamlıbağ.teaser: The house whose own history begins in 1925, with a workshop bought from a Greek winemaker
bars:Çamlıbağ.story: By its own account, and a Bilkent University study of the family, Çamlıbağ began in 1925, when the Yunatçılar family bought a Greek winemaker's workshop as the island's Greek growers were leaving; the history fold tells that story. Wine writers note that it and Talay are related families. What you visit today is a working shop in town, shelves of native-grape bottles and staff who know them, not a show cellar: the place to buy Vasilaki and Karalahna by the case for the boat.
bars:Çamlıbağ.why: Buy here for the boat: the island's grapes from one of its oldest houses, at shop prices.
